facts.claim: RFC 5322 says the From field names the author of a message: the person or system responsible for writing it. Nothing in it proves who that is.
RFC 5321 says each mail server that takes a message must add a Received line at its top, and the server that makes final delivery adds a Return-Path line holding the envelope sender.
RFC 5321 says a sending server first looks up the MX record of the recipient’s domain to find which server to hand the message to.
RFC 7208 has SPF check the envelope sender’s domain (MAIL FROM) against the IP address of the server handing the message over, and caps a check at 10 DNS lookups.
RFC 7208 says receivers should not reject mail on a softfail alone, and must treat neutral like no record at all.
RFC 6376 has the signer name its domain (d=) and a selector, and publishes the public key in DNS at <selector>._domainkey.<domain>.
RFC 6376’s relaxed canonicalisation tolerates common changes such as replaced whitespace and rewrapped header lines.
RFC 7960 notes that mailing lists often tag the subject or add a footer, and any such change breaks the DKIM signature.
RFC 7489 counts an SPF or DKIM pass for DMARC only when its domain aligns with the From domain, relaxed by default, and offers three policies: none, quarantine and reject.
Gmail’s sender guidelines say that from February 1, 2024, anyone sending more than 5,000 messages a day to Gmail must set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC (policy none allowed), with the From domain aligned.
Yahoo’s sender best practices required bulk senders, from February 2024, to use both SPF and DKIM and publish a DMARC policy of at least p=none, with the From domain aligned.
